steps.title: Building compound adjectives
steps.html:
What they are. Two words joined, usually by a hyphen, working together as one adjective: thick-rimmed, home-made, second-hand. English builds them freely, which is why you meet ones that are in no dictionary.

The common patterns. Adjective + past participle (clean-shaven, little-known); adverb + past participle (well-educated); adjective + present participle (tight-fitting, long-lasting); noun + past participle (home-made, hand-written); noun + noun (fixed-wheel, retro-style).

Never plural. Whatever the meaning, the compound does not change: thick-rimmed glasses (two rims), a six-month delay (six months), a two-hour film. The plural sits on the noun that follows.

Hyphen or not. Before a noun, hyphenate: a well-known band. After the verb, usually no hyphen: the band is well known. After an -ly adverb, never hyphenate: a brightly coloured dress, because -ly already shows the words belong together.

Order. The compound counts as one adjective and takes one slot in the sequence from lesson 41: a large black fixed-wheel bike.

When you cannot remember one. Use the vague language from this lesson: a sort of one-gear bike, the kind of glasses with thick frames. It is normal, it is fast, and it keeps the sentence moving.

steps.title: The commonest errors at this level
steps.html:
• thick-rimmeds glasses or a six-months delay — never plural.
  • a brightly-coloured dress — no hyphen after -ly.
  • hand-second — the order inside the compound is fixed.
  • tight fitting jeans before a noun — the hyphen is needed.
  • renowned of — it is renowned for.

steps.title: Напиши свой текст
steps.sub: Напиши ответ, затем сверься с образцом
steps.modelHtml:
You would know one from the shoes. Everything else about the climbing crowd at our local wall is deliberately ordinary — loose trousers, a plain T-shirt, nothing branded if they can help it — but the shoes are tight-fitting to the point of pain, brightly coloured, and usually second-hand from somebody two sizes down. Nobody who is serious buys new ones.

The equipment tells you more than the clothes. It is a low-tech crowd in a high-tech city: chalk bags that somebody’s mother sewed, home-made finger-training boards, hand-written notebooks of routes going back years. There are three or four people with expensive watches and everyone else treats them, kindly, as tourists. They mend things. A worn rope becomes a dog lead and then, eventually, something else.

What they are against is harder to say and it is the real thing. They are suspicious of anything that turns climbing into a product: competitions, sponsorship, gyms with branded lighting, obscure grading systems that only make sense on a screen. They talk about little-known crags the way other people talk about restaurants, and they genuinely do not want the crags to become renowned. The word they use for the mainstream version is “plastic”, which is unfair, and they know it is unfair, and they keep saying it.

What this description misses is that most of them would object to being described at all. If I had asked permission to write it, I would have got four different accounts and one flat refusal, and the refusal would have been the most accurate of the five.
